messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Initialisation suggestion
parts: I've dealt with some models where Stan / NUTS gets to roughly the right region within a few iterations, and others where it might take 500 or 1000 very low treedepth iterations, and then move on to treedepth 10 or 12. It's difficult to specify the right number of iterations for such problems. I realise there may be ways to parameterise the model to change this behaviour, but it would also be pleasant if one could pass an additional parameter delineating some sort of variable length init phase, that ended once x iterations have passed since observing the highest likelihood.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
parts:
After the refactor to the low-level commands, we'll have
much more flexibility in starting and stopping so will be
able to start exploring some more flexible adaptation
strategies. What we'll want to do is something like split
R-hat to assess whether the adaptation paths
have "converged" (they're not Markov chains, so the usual
definitions don't quite apply).

Our adaptation is enough like sampling that this may work.

Just doing something in a single adaptation path
based on the log density (it's usually log likelihood + log prior)
is tricky because we're looking for the high mass volume of the
posterior for sampling, not the mode.

I really need to finish my case study on typical sets and
the curse of dimensionality so we have some clear examples
to illustrate why the mode is often atypical.

- Bob

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
parts: Ok sounds good. I understand your point that it's difficult to determine convergence given a single path and log density - my suggestion was not to determine convergence, more to amend this as a first variable length initialization stage, and to move on to 'regular initialisation / warmup' after a few iterations where the log density is no longer increasing. But I'm happy if you have bigger and better plans for this sort of problem. In the meantime when this is a problem I've decided to optimize, with hyper variances fixed at a medium to high values, to determine start values... something that will probably induce head shaking from a few but is working well in these cases.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
parts:
We're happy to have people experiment with alternative
initialization schemes. We need to estimate a step size
and mass matrix (diagonal by default). The mass matrix
is basically an inverse covariance --- in the diagonal case,
it determines step sizes in each parameter dimension.

It'd be great if we could get to the typical set more quickly.
The challenge is the usual chicken-and-egg problem: in order
to move efficiently, we need the mass matrix and step size
and in order to get the mass matrix and step size, we need to
be able to move efficiently. The problem is exacerbating
by models with varying posterior curvature, as the optimal
mass matrix and step size will vary by region, so we really need
something conservative enough to work globally in the typical
set of the posterior.

What we do now is alternate running the sampler for increments
of exponentially increasing size, estimate the covariance
from the last increment, then find a step size that meets
the acceptance rate criterion (not simple Metropolis for NUTS),
then keep going. We want to keep adapting until the covariance
and step sizes reach equilibrium.

We could try something like finding a posterior mode, but the
problem with that is most of the multilevel models we use don't have
posterior modes---the density is unbounded as you head to
zero multilevel variance. So it's not clear where to stop.

- Bob

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
parts:
We could try something like finding a posterior mode, but the
problem with that is most of the multilevel models we use don't have
posterior modes---the density is unbounded as you head to
zero multilevel variance.  So it's not clear where to stop.

Right, though at least in the cases I've tried, optimizing with the multilevel variances fixed to the mean of their prior is working well for providing inits. This is done quite hackily by just modifying the loglik and gradient functions I pass to the optim function in R (such that no matter what parameters are passed in by optim, the multilevel variance subset are always fixed), but that seems to be working...
